s0101.literal: He even called in distant and near, mustered strength in Ba and Xiang, and his partisans ranged abroad, plundering Yi and She.
s0101.idiomatic: He even rallied allies far and near, gathered force in Ba and Xiang, and sent his factions to ravage Yi and She.

s0102.literal: Moreover a separate column under Ouyang He and others pressed Hengzhou; south of the ranges all was turmoil, and the months dragged on.
s0102.idiomatic: Another column under Ouyang He and others besieged Hengzhou; the south of the mountains was in turmoil for many months.

s0103.literal: His guilt exceeded that of the Prince of Changyi; his infamy was worse than that of Emperor Taihe.
s0103.idiomatic: His crimes outdid the deposed Prince of Changyi; his name was fouler than Emperor Taihe's.

s0104.literal: Yet though the wicked leaders were dead and the evil bands scattered, day by day We looked for reform, yet he only concealed it the more; defying ritual and forgetting virtue, his nature would not mend—he delighted in calamity and plotted disorder, savage and stubborn without end.
s0104.idiomatic: Though the ringleaders were dead and their gangs broken up, We still waited for him to mend his ways, but he only hid his faults; scorning ritual and virtue, he would not change—he loved trouble and schemed rebellion, fierce and unrepentant.

s0105.literal: Zhang Anguo, petty, fierce, and cunning, was reduced to a small bandit, yet still sent his man Jiang Yu to lure men out of the upper capital, set up a mobile headquarters, and choose vicious accomplices.
s0105.idiomatic: Zhang Anguo, mean, violent, and sly, had shrunk to a petty robber, yet still sent Jiang Yu to draw men from the capital, set up a field headquarters, and pick out hardened criminals.

s0106.literal: Jiao's wife Lu, condemned to pounding as punishment, was taken in from the
s0106.idiomatic: Jiao's wife Lu, sentenced to labor at the mortar, was received from the

s0108.literal: Editorial footnote marker 12. offices and hidden in the Everlasting Lane, that she might win over kin and friends and plot deadly harm.
s0108.idiomatic: Editorial footnote marker 12. palace offices and hidden in the Everlasting Lane to win over kin and friends and plot murder.

s0109.literal: The steward Hou Faxi and others, under the Grand Tutor's command, constantly moved in and out of the princely mansion; fed with deep profit, they plotted trouble at the armpit.
s0109.idiomatic: The steward Hou Faxi and others, who served in the Grand Tutor's household and frequented the court, were bought with heavy bribes to strike at close range.

s0110.literal: Then again the steward Sun Tai and others secretly linked together, with great traffic between them; their military strength was very strong, and they fixed a date to raise disorder.
s0110.idiomatic: Then the steward Sun Tai and others secretly joined them; their traffic was heavy and their forces strong, and they set a day for revolt.

s0111.literal: The royal house has fortune; its span is far; Heaven guided their hearts, and all alike were exposed.
s0111.idiomatic: The dynasty is blessed with long fortune; Heaven moved their hearts, and the plot came to light together.

s0112.literal: These documents We now show you—if this can be borne, who could endure it?
s0112.idiomatic: We now show you these documents—if this can be tolerated, who could bear it?

s0113.literal: The ancestral foundation will fear collapse and ruin—how can We again perform the solemn suburban sacrifices and face the myriad people?
s0113.idiomatic: The ancestral foundation would totter—how could We still perform the great sacrifices and rule the people?

s0114.literal: Following precedent, he should be sent into exile; now let him be specially demoted to Prince of Linhai and sent back to his princely residence.
s0114.idiomatic: By ancient precedent he belongs in exile; let him therefore be demoted to Prince of Linhai and sent to his fief.

s0115.literal: The Grand Tutor, Prince of Ancheng, Xu, by nature possesses virtue; sagely and broad, the two empresses set their hearts on him, and the three spirits look to him in hope.
s0115.idiomatic: Grand Tutor Xu, Prince of Ancheng, is virtuous by nature, sage and far-reaching; both empresses trust him, and heaven and earth mark him out.

s0116.literal: Since the previous reign's discontent he has held overall charge of the state; authority and kindness were proclaimed together, punishments and ritual alike established; at his command Xiang and Ying were cleared, and opening territory and expanding borders, Jing and Yi bowed to the wind—like Taiwu continuing Yin, or Zhongdu serving the house of Han; compared for merit and fame, how could the rest even be glimpsed?
s0116.idiomatic: Since the last reign's troubles he has governed the realm; power and grace went together, law and ritual alike; at his word Xiang and Ying were pacified, and in opening lands Jing and Yi submitted—like Taiwu carrying on Yin, or Zhongdu upholding Han; beside his merit and fame, who else even comes close?

s0117.literal: Moreover the earth revealed a spirit seal and heaven showed a long comet; removing the old and establishing the new, auspicious signs all appeared.
s0117.idiomatic: The earth has shown a sacred seal and heaven a long comet; omens of renewal have all appeared.

s0118.literal: The Literary Emperor knew his son's measure, a matter like Emperor Yao's; his wish to pass the throne to his younger brother also matched Duke Tai of Wu.
s0118.idiomatic: Emperor Wen knew which son could bear the charge, as Yao did; his wish to pass the throne to his younger brother matched the Duke of Wu.

s0119.literal: Now his former intent may again be carried out; establish the worthy ruler and exalt the sage lord, that the ancestral temple may be secured and the stars held firm.
s0119.idiomatic: Let his former intent now be fulfilled: raise the worthy prince and secure the temple, that the throne and the heavens may stand firm.

s0120.literal: Within and without should follow the old statutes and welcome the imperial carriage.
s0120.idiomatic: Court and command should follow the old rites and welcome the new emperor.

s0121.literal: We, the unworthy, have unhappily met this deep grief; without this high change, how could the altars of state be kept from peril—how could We bow at the high shrine or return the late emperor to the martial park?
s0121.idiomatic: We, the bereaved, have met this heavy sorrow; without this great change the state could not stand—how could We worship at the high shrine or lay the late emperor in the martial tomb?

s0122.literal: Taking up the brush, Our feelings are torn between grief and joy.
s0122.idiomatic: As We set brush to paper, Our heart is torn between sorrow and relief.

s0123.literal: That day he moved out to a separate residence.
s0123.idiomatic: That same day he left the palace for a separate residence.

s0124.literal: In the fourth month of the second year of Taijian he died, aged nineteen.
s0124.idiomatic: In the fourth month of Taijian year 2 he died, aged nineteen.

s0125.literal: The emperor was benevolent and weak and lacked the capacity of a ruler; Emperor Wen always feared he could not sustain the enterprise. As legitimate heir of the principal consort, the matter of deposition was weighty, and so for many years he hesitated.
s0125.idiomatic: The emperor was mild and feeble and lacked a ruler's stature; Emperor Wen long feared he could not bear the burden. As legitimate heir of the chief consort, deposing him was grave, and for years he could not decide.

s0126.literal: When his illness was about to reach its crisis, he summoned Emperor Xuan and said, "I wish to follow the affair of Duke Tai," Emperor Xuan at first did not grasp his meaning; afterward he understood, then bowed prostrate, wept, and firmly declined.
s0126.idiomatic: As his illness deepened he called Emperor Xuan and said, "I mean to follow the Duke of Wu's example of yielding the throne." At first Emperor Xuan did not understand; when he did, he prostrated himself, wept, and refused.

s0127.literal: Afterward Dowager Empress Xuan carried out the edict and deposed the emperor.
s0127.idiomatic: Later Dowager Empress Xuan carried out the will and deposed him.

s0128.literal: The historian says: Though Linhai bore the weight of succession, he was benevolent, mild, and Confucian-weak; Editorial footnote marker 13. blending right and wrong, undisturbed by gain or loss—he was of the sort of Emperor Zhi and Emperor Hui of Han.
s0128.idiomatic: The historian writes: Though Linhai held the heir's place, he was gentle, mild, and timid in the Confucian way; Editorial footnote marker 13. he blurred right and wrong and was unmoved by gain or loss—in the line of Emperor Zhi and Emperor Hui of Han.

s0129.literal: Emperor Wen knew the weight of the sacred vessel and that it was hard to bear; deeply discerning Yao's intent, he did not pass on the precious throne.
s0129.idiomatic: Emperor Wen knew how heavy the throne was and that this son could not carry it; reading Yao's intent, he did not hand him the mandate.

s0131.literal: On gengxu day of the eighth month he was established as crown prince—comment: "eighth month, gengxu day"
s0131.idiomatic: On "eighth month, gengxu day, established as crown prince"—note:

s0136.literal: [ji] mao—changed according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0136.idiomatic: [ji] mao—emended per the History of the Southern Dynasties.

s0137.literal: Comment: that month dingchou was the first day of the month; there was no yimao.
s0137.idiomatic: Note: that month began on dingchou; yimao does not occur.

s0138.literal: the newly appointed Central Protector General Shen Ke was made Protector General—"Ke" was originally corrupted to "Lue"; all editions are not corrupt; now corrected.
s0138.idiomatic: On "newly appointed central protector general Shen Ke made protector general": the text originally read Lue for Ke; other editions are correct; emended.

s0139.literal: Comment: according to Ke's main biography, in the sixth year of Tianjia he was central protector general and soon moved to protector general.
s0139.idiomatic: Ke's biography records that in Tianjia year 6 he was central protector general and shortly after became protector general.

s0140.literal: Autumn, seventh month, dingyou—"Autumn, seventh month," the three characters, were originally ink lacunae; now supplied according to the Basic Annals of the Deposed Emperor in the History of the Southern Dynasties and the Comprehensive Mirror.
s0140.idiomatic: On "autumn, seventh month, dingyou": the three characters autumn seventh month were ink lacunae in the original; supplied from the Southern Dynasties annals of the Deposed Emperor and the Comprehensive Mirror.

s0141.literal: Comment: in all editions it reads "autumn, eighth month"—erroneous.
s0141.idiomatic: All editions read autumn eighth month—an error.

s0142.literal: That year in the eighth month yisi was the first day of the month; there was no dingyou.
s0142.idiomatic: That year the eighth month began on yisi; dingyou does not occur.

s0143.literal: the two sovereigns shone in succession and the nine regions were all governed—"shone nine" the two characters were originally ink lacunae; now supplied according to all editions.
s0143.idiomatic: On "two sovereigns shone in succession and the nine regions were governed": the two characters shone nine were ink lacunae; restored from other editions.

s0144.literal: spread the late emperor's grace—"spread" the character was originally an ink lacuna; supplied according to all editions.
s0144.idiomatic: On "spread the late emperor's grace": spread was an ink lacuna; restored from other editions.

s0145.literal: the Prince of Shixing, Bomao, General Who Campaigns East, opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes, and Inspector of East Yangzhou, was made Central Army General—"General Who Campaigns East"
s0145.idiomatic: On "Prince of Shixing Bomao, general who campaigns east, opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes, inspector of East Yangzhou, made central army general"—note on general who campaigns east:

s0147.literal: in the third year of Tianjia reads "General Who Garrisons the East," the same as the main biography.
s0147.idiomatic: Tianjia year 3 reads general who garrisons the east, matching his biography.

s0148.literal: "Central Army General" in the main biography reads "Central Commander General."
s0148.idiomatic: His biography reads central commander general for central army general.

s0151.literal: [zhou] for those misled by Jiao—changed according to the History of the Southern Dynasties.
s0151.idiomatic: [zhou] for those misled by Jiao—emended per the History of the Southern Dynasties.

s0152.literal: General Who Pacifies the South and Inspector of Xiangzhou Wu Mingche, on his present title, became opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes and was advanced in title to General Who Garrisons the South—comment:
s0152.idiomatic: On "Wu Mingche, general who pacifies the south and inspector of Xiangzhou, on his present title made opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes and advanced to general who garrisons the south"—note:

s0154.literal: In the first year of Taijian there is again the passage "the newly appointed General Who Pacifies the South, opener of the mansion equal to the three dukes, and Inspector of Xiangzhou Wu Mingche was advanced in title to General Who Garrisons the South"; the main biography also says "in the first year of Taijian he was appointed General Who Garrisons the South"—it is suspected that the six characters "was advanced in title to General Who Garrisons the South" here are intrusive.
s0154.idiomatic: Taijian year 1 again has Wu Mingche, newly appointed general who pacifies the south with a mansion equal to the three dukes and inspector of Xiangzhou, promoted to general who garrisons the south; his biography agrees. The six characters promoted to general who garrisons the south here are probably intrusive.

s0155.literal: In the last days of Liang's mandate—"mandate" was originally corrupted to "way"; all editions are not corrupt; now corrected.
s0155.idiomatic: On "in the last days of Liang's mandate": the text originally read way for mandate; other editions are correct; emended.

s0158.literal: [offices]—"palace" should read "offices"; all editions alike are in error; now changed.
s0158.idiomatic: On [offices]: palace should read offices; all editions err; emended.

s0159.literal: benevolent, mild, and Confucian-weak—"Confucian" in all editions reads "cowardly."
s0159.idiomatic: On "benevolent, mild, and Confucian-weak": all editions read cowardly for Confucian.

s0160.literal: Comment: ru has the sense of cowardly weakness; all editions read "cowardly," and it is suspected that later men arbitrarily changed it.
s0160.idiomatic: Note: ru can mean timid; the reading cowardly may be original, and Confucian a later change.
